description:
Taipei team on "Abandoned but not Forgotten." Some hardware NASA left on the Moon still does science today. We will tell that story to kids with real NASA data, like a diary.

We bring product and storytelling lead, fast coding, and NASA data already tested.

Looking for: illustrator, 2D animator, English writer or narrator, and anyone who teaches science to kids.

Chinese and English. Taiwan teammates welcome (local awards need half the team to be ROC nationals).
summary:
Astronauts left a mirror on the Moon in 1969. It needs no power, and telescopes on Earth still aim lasers at it.

Still Answering is a 15-page picture book on the web, told by that mirror, for kids aged 10 to 15. You time a real laser shot to the Moon and back in its real 2.60 seconds, see why so little light comes back, and look up whether the mirror answered on your birthday. Every shot is a real record from NASA's CDDIS archive.

The challenge asks for the story of something left behind and what it made possible. This mirror is still part of an experiment today, so we let its own records tell the story.

We made it because the astronauts left, but the experiment never stopped. We wanted a 12-year-old to feel that, not just read it.

Two pages to try first: the stopwatch, https://still-answering.pages.dev/#p3, and the birthday search, https://still-answering.pages.dev/#p12
details:
Live site: https://still-answering.pages.dev

Code and data: https://github.com/a96020183/still-answering

Try these two pages first: the stopwatch (https://still-answering.pages.dev/#p3) and the birthday search (https://still-answering.pages.dev/#p12).

WHAT IT IS

Apollo 11 left a laser mirror on the Moon in 1969. It needs no power, and telescopes on Earth still aim lasers at it. Still Answering is a 15-page picture book on the web, told by that mirror, for kids aged 10 to 15. It takes about five minutes on a phone.

WHAT YOU DO

- Page 3: you time a real laser shot. A telescope in New Mexico fired it on June 6, 2026. The light flies to the Moon and back in its real 2.60 seconds, and you press Stop at the ding.

- Page 5: the seismometer left next to the mirror stopped taking commands after 37 days. The mirror needs no power, so it still works.

- Page 6: you drag a flashlight and see why a glass corner sends light straight back.

- Page 7: a real shot from 1969, Texas. Earth tried 550 times. The telescope caught 8.

- Page 9: you guess first, then watch two real nights side by side. The light came back 0.35 seconds sooner on the night the Moon was closer.

- Page 10: the Moon drifts away about 3.8 cm a year, about one glass corner.

- Pages 12 to 14: you enter your birthday and the book looks for a record on that day. If there is none, it says so ("not in the records we have") and plays the nearest real answer. You leave with a card, and a Moon card that shows the Moon lit as it was on that day.

Each hands-on page ends with a Think question. Each chapter has a source panel with a picture, a short note and full references, and a one-page classroom guide. In class mode, the whole class votes before the stopwatch.

WHY YOU CAN TRUST IT

Every laser shot is a real record from NASA's CDDIS archive, and the same files are in our repo. We wrote our own model of the light's trip and fitted nothing to the laser data. Over all 107 Apollo 11 records from 2022 in our snapshot, the model and the measurement differ by 0.49 m, one way, at a distance of about 384,400 km. A version of the model fixed before we looked was off by 0.021 m and 0.271 m on two 2026 records it had never seen. One command, python scripts/reproduce.py, reruns the numbers.

WHO HAS TRIED IT

On 2026-11-15 two adults tried an early version and found four problems: it said too late who "I" is, it did not say who "two of us" are, page 9 gave nothing to do, and the chapters jumped. All four are fixed. That evening two children and four adults played the current book in two to seven minutes. Their stopwatch tries were off by 0.06 to 0.66 seconds, and one child got closer every time: 0.5, 0.4, then 0.3 seconds. Four of the six could say in one sentence what it is about, and one child saved the birthday card. What they told us led to a shorter page 8, pictures in the source panels, quicker links on the last page and the Moon card.

WHAT NEXT

- Say more plainly at the start what the reader will do, and why page 12 asks for a birthday. Two adults found this unclear at first.

- Add the other four mirrors: Apollo 14, Apollo 15, Lunokhod 1 and Lunokhod 2. Their records are in the same archive, and our code already handles them.

- Run a classroom trial with teachers, using the one-page guide.

ACCESSIBILITY

It works with the sound off: every line is on screen, and the Stop button turns gold when the light returns. It works with the keyboard and with reduced motion. Images have text descriptions. There is no login and no download, and nothing is loaded from other sites. It has not been tested with a screen reader yet.

HOW WE MADE IT

Python with NumPy, SpiceyPy, PyERFA and Matplotlib for the data and the model. HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript for the book, with Canvas and SVG drawings and Web Audio for the dings. three.js, Playwright and FFmpeg render the 3D cover loop, the film and the Moon images. The site is hosted on Cloudflare Pages. Claude Code, an SI coding assistant, wrote the code under our direction, and every drawing made by that code is labelled "SI-assisted" on screen. The voice is a human recording by Lin Ting-ju.
